\chapter{Standing Vowels}
\label{ch:mr-ubhe-svara}
\hlchaptermodality{65}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can write the four vowel letters that begin a word, and say which of them a word needs rather than the sign that hangs on a consonant.}

From cold, with nothing open: write the four standing vowels this chapter taught, in the order they were met.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[ii]{\mr{ई} — the long one, standing on its own}

\label{lesson:MR-W65-ii-independent}



\begin{quote}
Draw the short standing \textbf{i}. Then draw the long \textbf{ii} sign, the one that hangs on a consonant and has been in your hand since the first chapter.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script}
\begin{quote}
\mr{ई}
\end{quote}

\textbf{\mr{ई}} is the long partner of \textbf{\mr{इ}}, and it is a \textbf{letter} rather than a sign.

\textbf{\mr{ईमेल}} — \emph{email}. The word opens with it, which is the one job a standing vowel has.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the sign rides, the letter stands}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{shape} & \textbf{where it goes} \\
\midrule
\mr{◌ी} & hangs on a consonant \\
\mr{ई} & stands at the start of a word \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\textbf{These are two shapes for one vowel, and which one you use is decided by what comes before it.} A consonant in front means the sound rides that consonant as a sign. Nothing in front means the sound needs a letter of its own to stand on.

You have been reading the sign since chapter one, at the end of a great many words. The letter is the same sound with nowhere to sit, and that is the whole difference between them.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Writing: guided copy}
Copy \textbf{\mr{ई}} twice with the model visible. Then write the \textbf{\mr{ी}} sign beside it and check that one of the two is standing alone and the other is waiting for a consonant to hang on.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which of \textbf{\mr{ई}} and \textbf{\mr{ी}} can open a word? (\textbf{\mr{ई}}.) What decides which of the two a word uses? (Whether a consonant is in front of the sound.)

Stroke order for \textbf{\mr{ई}} is illustrated in the Devanagari letter-order animations held by Wikimedia Commons.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[o]{\mr{ओ} — the same trade, a second time}

\label{lesson:MR-W65-o-independent}



\begin{quote}
Draw the \textbf{o} sign that hangs on a consonant. Then say what the lesson before this one did with a sign of the same age.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script}
\begin{quote}
\mr{ओ}
\end{quote}

\textbf{\mr{ओ}} is the standing form of the \textbf{o} you have been hanging on consonants since chapter one.

\textbf{\mr{ओठ}} — \emph{a lip}. Two letters, and you can read both.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the same arrangement you met a lesson ago}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{sign} & \textbf{letter} \\
\midrule
\mr{◌ी} & \mr{ई} \\
\mr{◌ो} & \mr{ओ} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\textbf{Two vowels, one arrangement.} A consonant in front means a sign; nothing in front means a letter. The reason this chapter is four short lessons rather than one long one is that the rule stays fixed while the shapes change, so what is worth practising is the shapes.

The two signs in the left column have been in your hand since the opening chapter. Their letters are arriving sixty chapters later, which is a gap worth noticing: a reader can spend a long time writing Marathi without ever needing to begin a word with a vowel.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Writing: guided copy}
Copy \textbf{\mr{ओ}} twice with the model visible. Then write the \textbf{\mr{ो}} sign beside it and read the pair aloud, letter then sign.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which shape does a word beginning with an \emph{o} sound need? (\textbf{\mr{ओ}}.) Which one does \textbf{\mr{ठ}} take when the \emph{o} rides it? (The \textbf{\mr{ो}} sign.)

Stroke order for \textbf{\mr{ओ}} is illustrated in the Devanagari letter-order animations held by Wikimedia Commons.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ai]{\mr{ऐ} — the letter a number was waiting on}

\label{lesson:MR-W65-ai-independent}



\begin{quote}
Draw the \textbf{ai} sign from the chapter where you met it. Then draw the standing letter from the lesson before this one.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script}
\begin{quote}
\mr{ऐ}
\end{quote}

\textbf{\mr{ऐ}} is the standing form of the \textbf{ai} sign, and this one has been holding up a word you need rather than only a class of them.

\textbf{\mr{ऐंशी}} — \emph{eighty}. It opens with \textbf{\mr{ऐ}}, so until this letter arrived the number could not be read at all.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: a sign that arrived late, and a letter that arrived later}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{sign} & \textbf{letter} \\
\midrule
\mr{◌ै} & \mr{ऐ} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

The \textbf{\mr{ी}} and \textbf{\mr{ो}} signs came in the first chapter. The \textbf{\mr{ै}} sign came far later, because a word needing it is rarer, and its letter is rarer still.

\textbf{That is why a gap like \mr{ऐंशी} sits unnoticed.} A number in the middle of a counting sequence looks like ordinary vocabulary, and nothing about it announces that one of its four shapes had never been drawn. The way such a gap gets found is by checking the letters a word needs against the letters a reader has met, rather than by reading the word and feeling that it looks familiar.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Writing: guided copy}
Copy \textbf{\mr{ऐ}} twice with the model visible. Then write the \textbf{\mr{ै}} sign beside it and check which of the two is standing alone.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which number opens with \textbf{\mr{ऐ}}? (\emph{Eighty}.) Could the \textbf{\mr{ै}} sign have done that job? (No — it needs a consonant in front of it.)

Stroke order for \textbf{\mr{ऐ}} is illustrated in the Devanagari letter-order animations held by Wikimedia Commons.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[au]{\mr{औ} — the last one standing}

\label{lesson:MR-W65-au-independent}



\begin{quote}
Draw the \textbf{au} sign. Then draw the standing letter from the lesson before this one, and say which number it opened.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script}
\begin{quote}
\mr{औ}
\end{quote}

\textbf{\mr{औ}} is the standing form of the \textbf{au} sign, and it is the fourth of four.

\textbf{\mr{औषध}} — \emph{medicine}. A word worth being able to read on a label, and one you could not have read an hour ago.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the four, and what they have in common}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{sign} & \textbf{letter} \\
\midrule
\mr{◌ी} \mr{◌ो} & \mr{ई} \mr{ओ} \\
\mr{◌ै} \mr{◌ौ} & \mr{ऐ} \mr{औ} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Four vowels the reader could hear and could hang on a consonant, and could not put at the front of a word. \textbf{The gap was never in the sound — it was in the position.}

That is the shape of this whole chapter. Where the script writes one vowel in two places, the two shapes look nothing alike, so a reader who has drawn the sign still meets the letter as something new.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Writing: guided copy}
Copy \textbf{\mr{औ}} twice with the model visible. Then write the \textbf{\mr{ौ}} sign beside it and read the pair aloud, letter then sign.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How many standing vowels did this chapter add? (Four.) Was the gap in the sound or in the position? (The position.)

Stroke order for \textbf{\mr{औ}} is illustrated in the Devanagari letter-order animations held by Wikimedia Commons.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ubhe svara]{standing vowels — four letters, from cold}

\label{lesson:MR-R65-standing-vowels}



\begin{quote}
Close the four lessons before this one. Draw the two signs you have had since the opening chapter, with nothing in front of you.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script: the four pairs, written out once}
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{sign} & \textbf{letter} \\
\midrule
\mr{◌ी} \mr{◌ो} & \mr{ई} \mr{ओ} \\
\mr{◌ै} \mr{◌ौ} & \mr{ऐ} \mr{औ} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Write the right column from memory. \textbf{One rule decides which column a word needs}: a consonant in front of the sound calls for the sign, nothing in front calls for the letter.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: what the four unlocked}]
\textbf{\mr{ऐंशी}} is \emph{eighty} and \textbf{\mr{औषध}} is \emph{medicine}. Neither could be read before this chapter, and neither is unusual — one is a number in the middle of a counting sequence and the other is on a label in every pharmacy.

\textbf{A word that looks ordinary can still be unreadable}, and the way to find out is to check its letters against the ones you have been taught rather than to look at it and feel that it seems familiar.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item which shape a word starting with an \emph{o} sound needs
  \item which shape \textbf{\mr{ठ}} takes when the \emph{o} rides it
  \item what decides between a sign and a letter
  \item the two words this chapter made readable
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How many of these four had a sign you already knew? (All of them.) Was the gap in the sound or in the position? (The position.)
\end{tcolorbox}
